problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have found a complete solution. The minimum number of tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{2025}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Structure of uncovered squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares forms a permutation matrix: there exists a bijection \(\sigma:\{1,\dots ,2025\}\to\{1,\dots ,2025\}\) such that the uncovered squares are \(\{(i,\sigma(i))\}\).

2. **Upper bound (construction).**  
   Choose \(\sigma(i)=i\) (the identity).  
   For each row \(i\) place a single rectangular tile covering all squares of that row except the diagonal cell \((i,i)\).  
   Each tile is a \(1\times2024\) rectangle; the tiles are disjoint, every row and column has exactly one uncovered square, and the total number of tiles is \(2025\).  
   Hence a tiling with \(2025\) tiles exists.

3. **Lower bound (rank argument).**  
   Represent the covered squares by the binary matrix \(A\) where \(a_{ij}=1\) iff \((i,j)\) is covered.  
   Then \(A = J - P\), where \(J\) is the all‑ones matrix and \(P\) is the permutation matrix of \(\sigma\).  
   By simultaneous row and column permutations, \(A\) is similar to \(J-I\); therefore \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(J-I)\).  
   The eigenvalues of \(J-I\) are \(2024\) (multiplicity 1) and \(-1\) (multiplicity 2024), so \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=2025\).

   Each rectangular tile corresponds to a rank‑1 binary matrix (outer product of its row‑indicator and column‑indicator vectors).  
   If the covering uses \(k\) tiles, then \(A\) is the sum of \(k\) rank‑1 matrices, giving \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\le k\).  
   Hence \(k\ge2025\).

4. **Conclusion.**  
   The construction uses exactly \(2025\) tiles, and the rank argument shows that no tiling can use fewer.  
   Therefore the minimal possible number of tiles is \(\boxed{2025}\).

---

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  
Consider the \(n\times n\) grid of unit squares.  
A *tile* is an axis‑parallel rectangle whose sides lie on grid lines; different tiles may not overlap (each unit square is covered by at most one tile).

#### 1. Form of the uncovered squares  

The requirement “each row and each column has exactly one uncovered unit square’’ forces the uncovered squares to be a *permutation matrix*.  
Indeed, there exists a bijection \(\sigma:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the uncovered squares are  

\[
U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

All other squares are covered.

Define the binary matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\) by  

\[
a_{ij}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }(i,j)\text{ is covered},\\
0 & \text{if }(i,j)\text{ is uncovered}.
\end{cases}
\]

Let \(J\) be the \(n\times n\) all‑ones matrix and let \(P\) be the permutation matrix corresponding to \(\sigma\) (i.e. \(P_{ij}=1\) iff \(j=\sigma(i)\)).  
Then  

\[
A = J - P. \tag{1}
\]

Row and column permutations do not change matrix rank, so \(A\) is similar to \(J-I\) (the case \(\sigma\) is the identity). Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(J-I). \tag{2}
\]

The eigenvalues of \(J\) are \(n\) (once) and \(0\) (multiplicity \(n-1\)). Subtracting the identity shifts each eigenvalue by \(-1\); thus the eigenvalues of \(J-I\) are  

\[
n-1\quad(\text{multiplicity }1),\qquad -1\quad(\text{multiplicity }n-1).
\]

All are non‑zero, so \(J-I\) is invertible and  

\[
\operatorname{rank}(J-I)=n. \tag{3}
\]

From (2) and (3) we obtain  

\[
\operatorname{rank}(A)=n=2025. \tag{4}
\]

#### 2. Upper bound: an explicit tiling with \(n\) tiles  

Choose the identity permutation \(\sigma(i)=i\); the uncovered squares are the diagonal cells \((i,i)\).  
For each row \(i\) place a single tile  

\[
T_i=\{(i,j)\mid j\neq i\},
\]

which is a \(1\times (n-1)\) rectangle covering every square of row \(i\) except the diagonal one.  
The tiles \(T_1,\dots ,T_n\) are pairwise disjoint because they occupy distinct rows.  

* Each row contains exactly one uncovered square \((i,i)\) by construction.  
* Each column also contains exactly one uncovered square, namely \((i,i)\) in column \(i\).  

Thus this arrangement satisfies all conditions and uses exactly \(n\) tiles. Hence  

\[
\text{minimum number of tiles}\le n. \tag{5}
\]

#### 3. Lower bound: rank argument  

Consider any admissible tiling consisting of \(k\) tiles \(R_1,\dots ,R_k\).  
For each tile \(R_t\) define its incidence matrix \(M_t\) by  

\[
(M_t)_{ij}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }(i,j)\in R_t,\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

Because a tile is a rectangle, there exist binary vectors \(u_t\in\{0,1\}^n\) (indicator of the rows of \(R_t\)) and \(v_t\in\{0,1\}^n\) (indicator of the columns of \(R_t\)) such that  

\[
M_t = u_t\,v_t^{\!\top}.
\]

Hence each \(M_t\) has rank 1 (over the real numbers).  
Since the tiles are disjoint and together cover exactly the squares counted by \(A\), we have  

\[
A = \sum_{t=1}^{k} M_t .
\]

The rank of a sum does not exceed the sum of the ranks, so  

\[
\operatorname{rank}(A) \le \sum_{t=1}^{k}\operatorname{rank}(M_t)=k. \tag{6}
\]

Using (4), \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\); therefore (6) yields  

\[
k \ge n = 2025. \tag{7}
\]

Thus any tiling must use at least \(2025\) tiles.

#### 4. Minimality  

From (5) we have a tiling with \(2025\) tiles, and from (7) no tiling can use fewer.  
Consequently the minimal possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{2025}.
\]
